articles.title: 1 Word To Describe Every NBA Team's First Week
articles.summary: Whew.
articles.body:
If you needed a single word to sum up the collective experience of the 2026-27 NBA season's opening week, that'd be the one.

We've had great games, thrilling comebacks and they-won-by-how-many?! blowouts. We've had so many how'd-he-do-that?! highlights, on both ends of the floor. We've had reasons for optimism, pessimism and everything in between.

And injuries. Goodness gracious, have we had injuries. You just hope for the best, brace for the worst and wish the worst kind of evil upon the injury bug. It's the least we can all do.

That's how things are going for all of us, but how was the first week for each of the 30 teams involved? Great question, let's find out one single-word description (some straightforward descriptions, others more word-association responses) at a time.

ATL | BOS | BKN | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

Atlanta's 2-0 start was erased by an 0-2 effort over two games in three nights against Houston. The Hawks have fared pretty well on both ends of the floor (they hound ball-handlers and plug up passing lanes as well as anyone), and their roster has struck great balance with scorers and ball-movers.

This defense is sitting 10th in efficiency and should only get better from here. The Hawks are still learning how to utilize their many stoppers without totally tanking the offensive spacing. They should crack that code at some point, especially if Jalen Johnson and Onyeka Okongwu find their three-point form.

The offense actually ranks higher ( eighth ), but that's the unit that gets and deserves more scrutiny. Atlanta doesn't have a superstar scorer or many fiery shotmakers, so you worry a bit about this bunch's ability to get big-time buckets in now-or-never situations.

The Celtics lost some of their margin for error when they swapped out Jaylen Brown for Paul George this summer. Particularly if Jayson Tatum isn't quite himself during his first full season back from a torn Achilles.

But if any team can number-crunch its way around that, it's probably this one. The Celtics are forever conscious of the fact that three is greater than two, and they've built their whole offensive premise around it.

They aren't quite the most three-happy team in hoops (fifth in attempts), but they don't have to be amid such a scorching start. They are first in both three-point makes (17.7) and percentage (42.4), a credit to the fact they have four different players averaging two-plus triples on 40-plus percent shooting.

Despite entering the campaign with contract-year Michael Porter Jr. still on the roster and adding Julius Randle this summer, the Nets are on the prowl for "the next Nets," as general manager Sean Marks told reporters this preseason. They know their future towers over their present in importance, so they're hoping to identify players who will be a part of it.

But how much does it help the future to have those young players stand around and watch Randle and Porter hoist more than 30 shots per game between them? It's not like the club is any more competitive (0-3 so far), it's just no longer in place to reap the rewards of the losing since Houston has swap rights on Brooklyn's 2027 first-round pick.

Mikel Brown Jr. is getting kid-glove handled amid cautions about the back injury that stunted his season at Louisville. Egor Dëmin isn't making many shots or plays. Save for maybe Nolan Traoré, the team's other three 2025 first-round picks are flopping. Things are off to a sleepy start for 2026 first-rounder Joshua Jefferson as well.

Week 1 Grades for Top Stars On New Teams 🌟

The Hornets are still awaiting the debuts of Kon Knueppel (hamstring) and Coby White (calf). And they obviously split from two starters over the offseason in LaMelo Ball and Miles Bridges.

Yet, here they stand holding a 3-1 record—that's almost entirely a product of a favorable schedule. They scored a quality victory over the Wizards on Monday, but otherwise they have single-digit wins over two winless teams in the Heat and the Nets and a 47-point drubbing at the hands of the Hawks.

The defense has been stingy-ish, but the offense has mostly been a mess. Three different starters are shooting below 40 percent (including Sion James' 19 percent ), and only two players on the roster are clearing 31 percent from three.

The Bulls took way too long to pull the plug on their last core, but they are finally fully committed to a youth movement. That should mean nothing but good things for their future, but it will also lead to a lot of present unsightliness.

So, rather than dwell on how brutally bad things have been ( minus-18.3 net rating! ), let's just soak up the electricity still resonating out of Caleb Wilson's 30-point, 14-rebound breakout.

Chicago is perpetually operating at 2X speed, partly because of its youth, partly because of how grotesque things can get for it in the half-court. What's fun about Wilson is that he's such a special athlete, he might still look sped up compared to everyone else even when the game starts slowing down for him.

The Cavaliers started their season by coughing up a 29-point lead against the Sixers. Then, they forced themselves to sweat out a four-point win over the lowly Nets by allowing 41 fourth-quarter points to one of the league's worst offenses.

And then, they wiggled out of a 15-point deficit to secure an overtime win over the previously unbeaten Timberwolves. It stands as one of the signature victories of the early season, as Cleveland manufactured its good fortune with balanced scoring, better offensive flow and a wildly impressive debut for rookie second-rounder Meleek Thomas.

The Cavaliers have probably learned very little about themselves so far, and they might not really gauge anything until the playoffs. James Harden needs to be more efficient, and Peyton Watson can't believe that was just said about someone other than him, but things feel familiar (for better and worse) in Cleveland.

The timeline disconnect between Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving is unavoidable. It's the reason folks can't stop speculating about an Irving trade , and the reason why such a swap might be the sensible move for the Mavericks to make at some point.

That said, the on-court connection already looks great. Flagg needed more scoring and creating support, and Irving is a ball-handling savant who can pile up points, orchestrate an offensive attack and still share the spotlight.

When Flagg and Irving have played, Dallas has gone 2-1 while posting a plus-7.2 net rating across 56 shared minutes. The hoops harmony impresses, even if it may not always be enough to keep these two tied together.

The Nuggets are three games into their season, and yet somehow already at the double-down stage of Nikola Jokić's response to hearing boos from their own fans.

This is not exactly the kind of stuff folks wanted to see from a club aiming to re-enter the contender ranks. Denver has two double-digit losses and one overtime win over New Orleans, which saw the Nuggets trail by 23 points and elicit those first rounds of boos.

The offense didn't show in the opener (84 points), and the defense has disappeared since (134.5 points allowed in the other two contests). Jamal Murray is hooping at a high level, and the second unit has found new sources for scoring (DeMar DeRozan) and energy (Trevon Brazile), but it's mostly been an uninspiring start.

Last season, the Pistons counted on Cade Cunningham to work his magic through crammed conditions inside the arc. Teams dared Detroit's shooters to beat them from distance and typically won that wager.

It's (obviously) early, but that's been an awful bet so far. The Pistons are prominently perched in the perimeter categories, sitting fourth in three-point makes (28th last season) and third in three-point percentage (17th). And to think, newcomer Isaiah Joe hasn't even found his rhythm yet (3-of-13).

Duncan Robinson is breathing fire (15-of-28), Daniss Jenkins is shooting on an ocean-sized rim (5-of-7) and John Collins can do no wrong from distance (7-of-14). This level of accuracy isn't sustainable, but any kind of marked improvement would be huge given how hard Cunningham was to handle with poor spacing and how dominant this defense can be.

The Warriors finally found their way to the win column, so that's something. And they even ran the Nuggets out of their own building while doing so. If nothing else, it was a reminder that Stephen Curry plus sufficient support can still add up to something special.

It's just that said support might require a nightly search, and a lot of them will come up empty. Kristaps Porziņģis might be forced into retirement , Jimmy Butler won't be back before the new year , Brandin Podziemski is inconsistent and Yaxel Lendeborg is a rookie— a fearless freshman , but still a rookie.

If Golden State hopes to make something out of Curry's final years, a trade might be needed to strengthen this roster. Then again, trading picks could be massively risky given all of the unknowns surrounding the team's future. These are already desperate times.

It might be happening, folks. With Fred VanVleet back to organize this group around him, Houston might be traversing that always treacherous jump from good to great.

The Rockets haven't had a gimme game on the schedule yet, and they're still 4-0 with an offense that routinely overwhelms. Alperen Şengün looks like an early MVP candidate, Kevin Durant is still Kevin Durant, Jabari Smith Jr. could push for 50/40/90 club entry and Amen Thompson is simultaneously playing within his limits on offense and challenging possibility's limits on defense.

Prior to last season, the Rockets looked like the kind of club where if everything broke just right, they could rank right alongside the elites of the elite. Then, VanVleet suffered a torn ACL, and things fractured in his absence. But if they're glued back together now, Houston's ceiling could be as high as ever.

Objectively speaking, it's been awesome to see Tyrese Haliburton work his way back onto the floor and mostly just look like himself. He missed all of last season while rehabbing a torn Achilles and is already flirting with a 50/40/90 slash line while dishing the second-most assists (9.5) and showing his trademark turnover avoidance (2.3).

He looks really good, and so do Pascal Siakam, Andrew Nembhard and Obi Toppin. But this roster, of course, runs deeper than that, and those other spots are either literally hurting (fingers crossed for Ivica Zubac's ankle) or hurting with their lack of production.

It feels like Indiana is just finding its footing and could return to top-tier status in the East at any moment. Then again, it's pretty far from that group so far with a nail-biter over New Orleans and losses to both Dallas and Milwaukee.

The Clippers looked cooked before the campaign even tipped.

Between the NBA's decision to strip them of five first-round picks following its salary-cap investigation—a finding the team disputed—and the delayed debut of Kawhi Leonard's replacement, Brandon Ingram, due to heel surgery and a partial Achilles tear, L.A.'s season seemed over before it started.

Since it actually started, though, the Clippers have looked pretty competitive. After throttling the lowly Sacramento Kings in the opener, L.A. then scrapped and clawed its way to respectable single-digit road losses to the Los Angeles Lakers and Oklahoma City Thunder (both undefeated).

The offense could use more layers, but upping Brook Lopez's interior action has been a smart move. The defense has played at a top-10 level ( eighth in efficiency), too, though it will need to get stingier around the basket ( fourth-most paint points allowed) for that to sustain.

The Lakers have clearly capitalized on a soft schedule to start. And even then, they had to wiggle out of double-digit holes against the Utah Jazz and Los Angeles Clippers. So, sure, there are ways to nitpick and reasons to be skeptical of this hot start.

All of that said, the Lakers are showing nothing short of offensive absurdity so far. They went out of their way to make it known this is Luka Dončić's team over the summer, and they've somehow increased that commitment since by tasking him with a preposterous (and surely untenable) 42.3 usage percentage. And he's responded by serving up the season's first 50-burger.

L.A.'s offensive numbers are ridiculous. The Lakers are grooving to the tune of a 125.9 offensive rating, a scoring rate 4.7 points per 100 possessions clear of last season's category leader. They've also amassed a sizzling (and silly) 68.2 true shooting percentage, which bests the No. 2 team by 5.4 percentage points. Wild .

With a soft schedule to start, some could have scripted a 4-0 opening for the Grizzlies. What they probably wouldn't have predicted was the pairing of that unblemished record with unsightly shooting rates from Cameron Boozer (29.5 percent) and Jerami Grant (37.5).

How is this happening? Ty Jerome. That's how. The 29-year-old, who hadn't averaged more than 12.5 points prior to last season (when he averaged 19.7 over 15 games), is popping off for 29.8 points per night while shooting 50.6 percent from the field and 37 percent from range.

Basketball-Reference has an MVP tracker that gives real-time, stat-based rankings "based on a model built using previous voting results." Jerome not only sits atop the tracker, his MVP probability is more than twice that of No. 2, Alperen Şengün.

Giannis Antetokounmpo's old team in Milwaukee has more wins than his new team in Miami. And the Bucks have only won once.

Antetokounmpo has been everything the Heat could have wanted and more. They, conversely, have looked even less capable of providing him with win-now support than the Bucks did ahead of their summer split. Miami gutted its roster to get Giannis to town, leaving the guard group severely undermanned and the offense uncomfortably reliant on Bam Adebayo.

Speaking of, what an abysmal start for the big fella: 11.8 points on 11.3 shots with a 40/16.7/61.5 slash line. Adebayo feels scapegoated for this team's sluggish start. The stat sheet says that scrutiny is justified.

When the Bucks were forced to trade Giannis Antetokounmpo this offseason, it seemed they lacked the leverage to ace their return. The package they ultimately accepted from the Miami Heat was viewed by some as unfavorable overall and by others as promising because of the long-term assets they collected.

The post-Giannis rebuild, it seemed, could take ages to come together. But maybe the plug-and-play pieces Milwaukee collected were much more impactful (relatively speaking) than it seemed.

Tyler Herro looks right at home piloting an NBA offense in his home state. Jaime Jaquez Jr. seems comfortable and capable as a second option. Kasparas Jakučionis could be a keeper. Ditto for Kel'el Ware, who's not even blocking shots or hitting from distance yet. The future already feels brighter, and that's without accounting for all of the other rebuilding assets on hand.

For a few magical hours Tuesday, this slide was dedicated to marveling at the Anthony Edwards-LaMelo backcourt and wondering whether it was already the NBA's best. ( Absolutely, by the way .)

But the basketball gods are adamant that no fun is allowed apparently, so we're now forced to pivot to this brutal update from ESPN's Shams Charania:

Arthroscopic surgery and a two-month absence aren't world-enders, obviously, but the NBA's can't-miss tandem is now missing in action and missing out on valuable chemistry-building time.

Edwards was looking like the best version of himself, and folks can only hope that's still the case on the other end of this injury. Ugh!

External expectations were effectively nonexistent for this team. In that sense, it can't be too surprising to see the Pels toting around a winless record.

Internally, though, there had to be at least some hope, right? Why else would they keep clinging on to the many coveted trade candidates on the roster? The front office sees something in this core, and it has almost made good on that potential; New Orleans' three losses have been decided by a total of nine points.

Still, it's losing games, and it isn't exactly paving the cleanest path for the future. Jeremiah Fears is struggling, Derik Queen is finding less floor time and nothing can be driving the trade values up for Trey Murphy III, Zion Williamson or Herbert Jones.

Something is up with the defending champion and winless Knicks. A championship hangover, perhaps? A few uncharacteristic barrages of bricks? Hard to say, but this banner-raising bunch is having a hard time finding its mark. New York is 29th in offensive efficiency, 29th in field-goal shooting and 28th in free-throw accuracy.

"There's no light switch we can just turn on and go and win the ballgame," Knicks skipper Mike Brown told reporters after his team fumbled a double-digit fourth-quarter lead against the Orlando Magic on Sunday. "Nobody's giving us anything, so we have to be better with the little things until we start shooting the ball."

As the tail end of that quote alludes to, the shooting will come around at some point. The Knicks had last season's fourth-best offense, and they're basically running back the same roster (minus backup big man Mitchell Robinson). These should be temporary challenges, but that doesn't make them any easier to watch.

This is a strange—and not at all fun—one to tackle. This is a full-fledged contender (and recent champion) flexing championship-level muscle: undefeated with the seventh-best net rating ( plus-10.3 ). Yet, it feels like none of that matters because OKC's wounds are too fresh.

Jalen Williams, the sidekick for Shai Gilgeous-Alexander when he's right, suffered a fractured fibula and dislocated left ankle Sunday. Cason Wallace, the team's new starter and designated chaos-creator on defense, exited the same contest with a torn labrum in his left shoulder. Both are slated for surgeries and facing months-long, maybe season-ending absences.

"We'll wrap our arms around these guys," Thunder general manager Sam Presti told reporters Monday. "We'll get them back, we'll get them healthy, but we got a lot of basketball to play in front of us. We got to put it together, figure out what the next steps are because this is part of the business that we're in."

Oklahoma City's roster runs deeper than most, but it isn't as deep as it was following the summer subtractions of Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe. The Thunder have several next-man-up candidates, but they don't have Williams or Wallace clones. This will be (and very much already is) tough.

The Magic are three games into the Sean Sweeney era. It certainly feels a lot like the chapters that preceded it.

The defense is better than the offense. A shooting shortage complicates everything this group wants to get done on the offensive end. The overlap between star wings Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner makes it difficult to simultaneously bring out their best. Oh, and there are multiple key contributors populating the injury report.

That about sums it up, right—both the first three games of this campaign and this entire core's existence.

Maybe Sweeney will figure out how to pull some new strings, and the schedule will ease up at some point, but it's hard to say when (if ever) Orlando fans should expect some relief.

The Sixers' new starting five is stacked with stars and maybe the best in basketball . You might think, then, that Philly would be pulverizing opponents from the start and building big enough leads for the stars to turn into late-game spectators.

That couldn't be farther from the truth. In reality, the Sixers have been pretty dreadful in the first frame ( minus-22.9 net rating) and then escape artists thereafter. They've already completed two double-digit comebacks, including rallying from 29 down against the Cleveland Cavaliers.

The Sixers would surely prefer not to stack up early-session stress sessions, and with the firepower in their opening group, they shouldn't have to. Still, there's something encouraging about seeing zero quit with this club, and no one should ever need reminding why to keep hope alive in tricky situations.

The Suns weren't good last season. They were better than expected, sure, but they lost 37 games and finished 15th in net rating, serving as play-in participants and then first-round fodder. And that was enough of an overachievement for Jordan Ott to land fifth in Coach of the Year voting.

Devin Booker doesn't have a co-star. No one else is averaging even 15 points at the moment. Yet, it's the defense sounding so many red-alert sirens, as it sits dead last in defensive efficiency.

The Suns shouldn't be (and probably aren't) this bad. They're still feeling the effects of that 41-point shellacking in the opener which started with Phoenix on the wrong end of a 21-0 run. But if they're just around average, then it's hard to make sense of their steadfast commitment to Devin Booker and harder to see how things can materially change given their severe lack of long-term assets .

It's only two games against Phoenix and Sacramento, but it's also two wins, a lot of offense, good results from the new backcourt and this-might-change-everything levels of offensive improvement from Toumani Camara.

The overloaded point guard group probably needs attention at some point, and stiffer competition could bring to life some of the obvious concerns with the Damian Lillard-Ja Morant pairing. And even if Camara is making his annual offensive leap, he's probably not actually an 18.5-point scorer and 61.9 percent shooter.

That said, if you're evaluating results, Portland's have been pretty great. The ball is moving, the shots are falling, the turnovers are kept to a minimum and the defense looks stingy. Encouraging start, for sure.

With the Kings lacking both win-now talent and long-term keepers, they don't have a lot of priorities going into these games. They're giving rookie Darius Acuff Jr. a neon-green light, and then hoping there are enough touches left over for Domantas Sabonis and Zach LaVine to produce at rates that will eventually attract a trade suitor.

Sacramento's future is all about Acuff, and the present pretty much reads the same. He has been given the freedom to feast buffet-style, and he is piling up all of the offensive possessions he cares to handle. His 34.0 usage percentage is fifth-highest among rotation regulars, and his 24.3 field-goal attempts are the fourth-most by a rookie ever.

This is pretty egregious chucking by someone converting fewer than 33 percent of their field goals and less than 15 percent from the perimeter, but the Kings don't have much else brewing, so why not?

The Spurs had one disaster quarter against the Thunder on opening night and later found themselves on the wrong end of the early (and heavy) favorite for the block of the year . For anyone wondering how the defending Western Conference champs are 1-2, that's the TL;DR explanation.

The broader summation highlights the challenges of adopting this three-guard lineup. Even if Stephon Castle has taken a sizable step forward as an outside shooter, there's still a slew of overlapping strengths and weaknesses between him, De'Aaron Fox and Dylan Harper. And promoting Harper to the first five has sapped a lot of steam out of this second unit.

Throw in some uncharacteristically rough shooting by Victor Wembanyama and Devin Vassell, and this is an offense that is very much coming together. It will figure things out—there's too much talent not to—but it clearly hasn't yet.

You know all of those long-limbed, mobile athletes the Raptors have plugged into their non-center spots? Well, they're all being fully unleashed amid a wave of relentless defensive disruption.

The Raptors are constantly getting their hands on something. Often times it's the ball, as their 25 deflections per outing lead the league by a mile (bigger gap between them and No. 2 than the one between Nos. 2 and 17). Some times it's the opponent, as their 27.7 fouls are also pacing the category.

There are some risk-reward elements with the approach, but the rewards are far outweighing the risks so far. Toronto has a tiny 97.8 defensive rating , while no one else is sitting below 100.5.

With tanking effectively off the table by lottery reform and an improved roster at the ready, this season was supposed to serve as Utah's springboard back to competitiveness. And perhaps it still will. So far, though, it's been a slog, and maybe a reminder that it's difficult to just flip the switch to competitiveness.

Speaking of difficulty, it's been a bumpy transition for No. 2 pick Darryn Peterson. He's also a 19-year-old rookie starter, so things are seldom smooth. That said, he could help himself by repurposing his shot diet and swapping mid-rangers for more attempts from point blank or the perimeter.

If all this wasn't enough, the Jazz also now face the difficult task of trudging forward without Jaren Jackson Jr., who might miss two months with a torn MCL in his right knee. And remember, they're already without Jusuf Nurkić, whose delay has been debuted by a foot injury suffered in Utah's preseason opener.

The Wizards are four games into this campaign and still awaiting the debut of No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa, who sprained his ankle in their preseason finale and hasn't suited up since. That puts a water-treading feel to everything else going on in the District.

There has been some legitimate fun, like opening night MVP chants for Anthony Davis or best-in-the-league playmaking from Trae Young (44 assists against nine turnovers). There's also been some not-so-fun stuff, like relentless targeting of Young on the defensive end and sporadic offensive involvement from young Wizards not named Kyshawn George.

It's all just part of the appetizer ahead of the main course, though. The Wizards are hoping Dybantsa will be their ultimate needle-mover, the star big wing who returns championship hopes to an organization that has so long lived without them. Seeing some proof-of-concept hints would give this fanbase a reason to get giddy.

Statistics used courtesy of NBA.com and Basketball-Reference.com and current through Monday's games.

articles.title: Week 1 Grades for LeBron, Giannis and NBA's Top Stars On New Teams
articles.summary: We have officially seen enough NBA basketball to start passing judgment on how the biggest names to change teams are faring in their new digs.
articles.body:
We have officially seen enough NBA basketball to start passing judgment on how the biggest names to change teams are faring in their new digs.

A week's worth of games doesn't lend itself to irreversible conclusions. But they give us an initial peek into what's working—and what's not.

Every possible angle will be considered when doling out grades. Early on, though, we focus more on each player's performance and fit relative to expectations than on team results.

First impressions are meaningful, even if they don't last. Let's see how Giannis Antetokounmpo, LeBron James, Jaylen Brown and more are doing one week into their new eras.

Giannis Antetokounmpo's monster stat lines ring hollow when the Miami Heat have yet to win a game.

Progress was made during the team's latest loss to the Dallas Mavericks, particularly on the defensive end . But it was still a loss. The Heat have still handedly lost the minutes he's played. They are still winless.

Giannis spitting out over 28 points per game while shooting over 70 percent at the rim means only so much when the offense feels functionally broken. He is averaging fewer true shooting attempts per 100 possessions in transition than last season and remains a wild card at the foul line (like the rest of Miami, apparently).

The fit with Bam Adebayo has been underwhelming so far. They don't have a ton of synergy and both want to occupy similar spaces. Bam has been forced to adjust. It's not been pretty. His effective field-goal percentage has plummeted by 25 points with Giannis on the floor.

To what extent the Heat's struggles fall on Antetokounmpo is debatable. New formations of this magnitude can take time. He doesn't come up with the defensive schemes. He didn't build the roster.

However, he is among those responsible for gutting it.

Four games into the season, the Minnesota Timberwolves have already been treated to every ounce of the LaMelo Ball experience.

The dazzling passes. The ball-handling sorcery. The unreal shot-making. Deep drives into the paint that make you believe in his physicality. Comfort coming off screens. Defensive engagement and playmaking that make you wonder whether it's time to adjust your priors.

Minnesota has also witnessed defensive lapses. A lack of physicality. Frustrating shot attempts. Foul trouble (against Toronto). Turnovers (against Cleveland). A lack of rim pressure. Over-dribbling.

Stark peaks and valleys are the LaMelo experience. Or rather, they're supposed to be. The Timberwolves are enjoying more peaks and a more even-keeled approach.

LaMelo has maintained an identical usage rate with and without Anthony Edwards, while more often than not deferring to his backcourt running mate. He's thrown more assists to Edwards than anyone else. The Wolves have an offensive rating of almost 140 when they share the floor.

Minnesota is also winning LaMelo's solo minutes, without notching a world-beater offense . Those stints are now mission critical with Edwards out at least two months.

The downside here still exists. We saw much of it in the Wolves' second-half performance against Cleveland, but it's getting harder and harder not to see this working out.

Jaylen Brown is at times getting lost in the Philadelphia 76ers' pecking-order shuffle.

Concrete efforts are made to feature Joel Embiid in full-strength lineups. LeBron James or Tyrese Maxey get the ball-handling reps before him. Brown's usage rate hasn't just dropped by nearly 11 point s since last season. It's at his lowest since 2019-20.

Brown still hasn't found his mid-range stroke, but he's traded those jumpers for more looks at the rim. His efficiency around the basket would be a career worst, but he's getting there more frequently than he has since 2018.

The three-ball falling at 42.1 percent clip is the bigger deal. Nearly 90 percent of all his makes from beyond the arc have come off assists. His two-point percentage has also soared to 67 percent when playing alongside the starters.

Head coach Nick Nurse has finagled lineups that let Brown tap into his on-ball leanings. Meanwhile, he has competed defensively, covering everyone from guards and forwards to big men.

As long as Brown doesn't have beef lamp chops-and-gravy with his role, this partnership between him and Philly will go down as a victory for everyone.

Despite not changing teams over the summer, Anthony Davis didn't make his Washington Wizards debut until this season. So, here he is. He looks better than expected.

Anyone who thought he was washed on the defensive end better tear up the receipts. He has held up pretty well on the perimeter and can still change shots around the basket. He's not contesting as many as we're used to, but that comes with (his preferred territory) spending so much time alongside another big.

Davis' offensive performance with Washington is uneven. He has turned in two huge scoring performances while building a genuine connection with Trae Young. He is shooting 70 percent at the hoop , but the overreliance on the mid-range game endures. He's made fewer than 25 percent of his twos away from the basket, which account for 45 percent of his field-goal attempts.

The Wizards have him spacing to the corner and popping or trailing out above the break on certain plays. Defenses generally don't care. Maybe his 3-of-6 clip from downtown against Charlotte changes that. History suggests it won't.

Spending most of his minutes with another big could end up capping both his and the team's offensive ceiling. Washington wants for spacing in its core lineups. Davis is shooting just 42.9 percent on twos when playing next to Alex Sarr or Deandre Ayton. So while Davis looks better than expected, you can't help but wonder whether he and the Wizards are deliberately leaving meat on the bone.

Paul George is comfortably clearing 25 points per game and shooting more threes than anyone in the league. His defense is so disruptive that it has nowhere to go but down.

It is more difficult at the moment to find cause for concern. Or something, anything, George is doing wrong.

A general lack of rim pressure isn't worth mulling over. The Boston Celtics knew this about him coming into the season. It hasn't prevented George from upping his shooting-foul rate in the early going. He clearly can't be used as a crunch-time crutch, but again, you don't acquire a 36-year-old expecting him to be something he hasn't been for a while.

George's 25 percent clip on long twos is worth filing away. Especially if they continue to account for one-quarter of his shots. He also wasn't much of an offensive factor in Boston's win over the New York Knicks, but it didn't impact his defensive energy.

Other than that and some questionable passes, Boston has to be thruh-illed with what it's seen from PG.

LeBron James is still trying to find himself within the Philadelphia 76ers' ecosystem. That constant search may end up being his new identity.

You can sense LeBron attempting to read the room across every game and lineup. He has defaulted to pass-always but cranked up the downhill juice on more than a few occasions, both in transition and when the Sixers are navigating drier spells.

Philly has lost the minutes LeBron has played so far. He's shooting 2-of-17 away from the rim , but the starting lineup is already gangbusters. Nearly two-thirds of his field-goal attempts have come at the hoop.

Even LeBron's defense is better than expected. The Sixers have used him to guard bigs at times, so Joel Embiid can roam. LeBron has also dabbled as a screener. He's sealed off guys around the basket. He's gotten out in transition, whether he's on or off the ball.

He's adapting and sacrificing at the same time.

This doesn't completely cancel out the individual efficiency. We're still talking about LeBron. The bar remains incredibly high. Shooting struggles and all, he's not exactly missing it.

Left knee swelling already cost Kawhi Leonard a game against the Minnesota Timberwolves and will sideline him for a period of weeks. His absence reminded everyone of his fragility, but it also reinforced how important he is to the Toronto Raptors.

Little came easy for the offense without him. Toronto averaged just 0.65 points per play in the half-court and posted a true shooting percentage below 48, according to Prime Stats.

The thing is, the version of Kawhi the Raptors need hasn't arrived yet. He is shooting under 35 percent on twos and less than 29 percent from three. He has yet to make an unassisted jumper from beyond the arc and has more turnovers than assists.

" You can't rush greatness " is something Kawhi actually said. It makes sense. He didn't have a traditional offseason. Much of it was spent waiting for his trade to go through amid the league's investigation into the Los Angeles Clippers allegedly circumventing the salary cap to funnel him extra money.

That has to take a mental toll—for which he's culpable—but also mess with his training regimen. At the very least, he didn't have access to the Raptors as early as he otherwise would have. Even now, you can tell he'll be fine on defense. Those hands are still big. The performance so far is poor, but not worth panicking over...yet.

Ja Morant is dispelling many of the concerns that left people ( including yours truly ) incredibly low on his fit with the Portland Trail Blazers.

Shooting over 37 percent from three was a good place for him to start. But he's also shifted away from the score-first mindset he held with the Memphis Grizzlies. His 15.4 field-goal attempts per 36 minutes would be a career low. Fewer of his made shots are going unassisted.

Though Morant isn't getting to the rim as much, the Blazers are generating tons of threes off his dribble penetration. He already has some chemistry with Deni Avdija, Toumani Camara and Robert Williams III. Portland is annihilating the opposition when he's playing alongside Damian Lillard.

Defensive concerns persist. The Blazers can't get by feasting on the sad-sack Phoenix Suns and Sacramento Kings forever. It remains to be seen how Morant will handle playing fewer minutes if they don't tick up from here. You'd like to see him get to the basket at a higher clip, finish better and draw more fouls.

Overall, though, the optimism arrow is trending upward.

Dan Favale is a National NBA Writer for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky ( @danfavale ), and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, co-hosted by Bleacher Report's Grant Hughes .

articles.title: LeBron James’ task in Philly bears a striking similarity to his new children’s book
articles.summary: LeBron James opens up to CNN Sports about his latest book, “Happy Spooky Halloween,” a story about kids working together to craft the perfect Halloween party.
articles.body: Attention Philly shoppers: When you’re hitting the candy aisle this week for Halloween provisions, be sure to stock up on Twizzlers, Mike & Ike’s, Snickers and Reese’s. Should LeBron James opt to park his helicopter on your front stoop to trick-or-treat, that’s what he’ll be looking for. So says James via an email interview with CNN Sports about his latest book, “Happy Spooky Halloween.” The book, a simple story about big kids and little kids working together to craft a Halloween party that finds the balance between scary and fun, could be a metaphor for his current condition. Rewriting the NBA pecking order while relocating from Los Angeles to Philadelphia and trading the Lakers’ gold standard for the 76ers’ un-Processing is a little scary. But if the big kids (James, Jaylen Brown and Joel Embiid) work together with the little kids (Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe and Anfernee Simons), it also might be a lot of fun. To be clear, James wasn’t penning an autobiography here. Main character Zara’s quick work toning down the overzealous fifth-grade cast of flying witches and hungry wolves required a lot less effort than taming the New York Knicks and the Boston Celtics. He was merely writing a book about one of his favorite holidays, one that conjures fond memories of running around Akron, Ohio, dressed up like his favorite horror movie characters – the haunting, bladed-glove-handed Freddy Krueger from “A Nightmare on Elm Street,” the shapeshifting creepy clown Pennywise from Stephen King’s “It,” and the hockey-masked stalker Jason Voorhees (props to James for using both names when he referenced him) from “Friday the 13th.” But in its pages, James was also hoping to find another way to connect with kids. “When I was little, I remember how much joy it brought me to get out of the house and trick or treat, just to see what other people are dressed up as and get a bunch of candy,” he said. “I think there’s so much to love about that experience of everyone coming out and enjoying that tradition with your community.” Helping kids, connecting with them and inspiring them has been an ongoing theme of James’ off-court life. He has penned four children’s books, and eight years ago, his foundation provided the funding for the I Promise School, an Akron-based elementary school for at-risk children that now includes grades one through eight. “We want to inspire kids to read more, and to be encouraged by stories they see themselves in,” he said. Without settling too comfortably into the psychiatrist’s armchair, it is easy to see why James’ own life might fuel such a hope. It’s hard to remember James’ beginnings anymore. He’s 41, so those early days feel like a lifetime ago. But they’re also a lifestyle ago, a foggy memory so incongruent with the present that it is hard to imagine that we’re talking about the same person. LeBron James is one-name famous, a crossover star who made his name and fortune in sports yet became so otherworldly at playing basketball that his singular name became part of the world’s lexicon. But before all that – before the four rings and the three gold medals, before the estimated $1 billion in endorsements and the helicopter taxi, before The Chosen One evolved into King James – he was just the son of a single mom, growing up in search of roots in Akron. LeBron James is one of the greatest basketball players in history and one of the world's most recognizable athletes. He has won four NBA titles over his 23-year career, most recently with the Los Angeles Lakers in 2020. He has also won titles with the Miami Heat and the Cleveland Cavaliers.In 2023, James became the NBA's all-time leading scorer, breaking Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's regular-season record of 38,387 points.In addition to being the NBA's all-time scoring king, James is also fourth all-time in assists and sixth in steals.On July 24, James announced that he would be playing for the Philadelphia 76ers for his 24th NBA season. With the benefit of hindsight, knowing what we now know about James, his origin story reads more like a tall tale. There’s the 9-year-old living with a local football coach who walked into the backyard in October 1994 and took to hooping like a duck to water, and there’s the peewee football star who scored 18 touchdowns in his first six-game season. There’s the high school star so popular that they moved his games to the University of Akron arena to accommodate the crowds, and of course the teenager who ended up on the cover of Sports Illustrated. James was, goes the narrative, born for this and borne into this. But it was not that linear. Not even close. Lost in the hyperbole and foreshadowing of greatness is the hard and ordinary stuff. The son of a loving single mom who struggled to make a way for the boy they called BronBron. Sleeping on sofas, cashing welfare checks for snacks, and relying on strangers’ kindness to take him in gave him some semblance of stability and structure. The elementary schooler so lost that, in one single year, he missed, according to ESPN.com, more than 100 days of school – not because he didn’t want to learn but in part because his life was so transient, he wasn’t sure which school to go to. Back then, he read the “Goosebumps” series as “an escape.” “Through books,” he told CNN Sports, “I could travel the world.’’ That inspired a life of curiosity, fueling an education not dissimilar to the one he’s trying to offer kids through his books. “I’m just a student of life and always want to learn new things,” he said. “So, I like to read about other people’s successes and journeys to see how they got to be where they are now.” He wasn’t being literal. But maybe have those sweets ready in case that candy-seeking helicopter shows up out front.

articles.title: Los Globetrotters volverán a España en 2027
articles.standfirst: Iniciarán una gira en mayo en el Movistar Arena de Madrid y recorrerán 9 ciudades más
articles.summary: Iniciarán una gira en mayo en el Movistar Arena de Madrid y recorrerán 9 ciudades más
articles.body: Tras celebrar su centenario, los legendarios Harlem Globetrotters dan comienzo a una nueva gira con Harlem Globetrotters: Rivales, que hará parada en España del 3 al 14 de mayo de 2027 y recorrerá diez ciudades: Madrid, Valencia, Sevilla, Málaga, Tenerife, Barcelona, Santiago de Compostela, Gijón, Bilbao y Mallorca. Esta nueva gira ampliará el universo de los Harlem Globetrotters con la incorporación de dos nuevos equipos rivales que se unirán a los históricos Washington Generals. Sus nombres e identidades se desvelarán en las próximas semanas, pero su llegada promete nuevos desafíos, enfrentamientos inéditos y más emoción sobre la cancha. Una evolución del espectáculo que mantiene intacta la esencia de uno de los equipos más reconocibles y queridos del mundo del deporte y el entretenimiento. Para esta edición los fans de los Harlem Globetrotters podrán disfrutar de su espectáculo con promociones exclusivas. La preventa, que transcurrirá desde hoy hasta el próximo 4 de noviembre, contará con un descuento especial del 20% a través de Mitaquilla.com. Una vez iniciada la venta general el 5 de noviembre, las entradas podrán adquirirse con un 15% de Una de las grandes novedades de Harlem Globetrotters: Rivales será el papel protagonista de los aficionados, que podrán participar activamente en el desarrollo del espectáculo a través de votaciones en directo para elegir determinados retos y desafíos. Además, algunos espectadores tendrán la oportunidad de saltar a la cancha para lanzar un tiro libre, convertirse en entrenadores por un cuarto o aparecer en el videomarcador gigante. Todo ello comenzará incluso antes del partido, gracias a una nueva fiesta de apertura gratuita que ofrecerá actividades interactivas, entretenimiento y experiencias para los asistentes desde el momento en que se abran las puertas del recinto. La experiencia también dará un paso adelante con una producción renovada, que incluirá nuevos contenidos en los videomarcadores, cámaras que mostrarán la perspectiva de los jugadores, interacciones con el público y narraciones en directo para acercar aún más a los aficionados a la acción y a la rivalidad entre los equipos. Con más de un siglo de historia, los Harlem Globetrotters continúan reinventando el espectáculo deportivo y acercando el baloncesto a públicos de todas las edades. Su combinación de talento, acrobacias, humor, interacción con los espectadores y desafíos sobre la cancha ha convertido al equipo en un fenómeno internacional que trasciende generaciones. Los míticos Harlem Globetrotters han protagonizado ya 11 giras con Proactiv Entertainment en España, y son los creadores más originales e influyentes del baloncesto actual, puesto en práctica por atletas con cualidades extraordinarias. Nicolás Renna, CEO de Proactiv Entertainment, destaca lo que significa para la compañía una conmemoración tan especial: "Los Harlem Globetrotters son mucho más que un equipo de baloncesto: son un icono mundial del entretenimiento y un referente capaz de sorprender a cada nueva generación. Es un orgullo seguir acompañándolos en su trayectoria y acercar al público español una nueva experiencia que, con la incorporación de nuevos equipos rivales y una mayor participación de los aficionados, promete llevar el espectáculo a otro nivel”.

articles.title: La crisis con China provocada por Mbappé ya la vivió la NBA
articles.standfirst: Un mensaje de Daryl Morey, dirigente de los Rockets, apoyando a Hong Kong en 2019 puso en serio peligro la relación comercial de la competición con el gigante asiático
articles.summary: Un mensaje de Daryl Morey, dirigente de los Rockets, apoyando a Hong Kong en 2019 puso en serio peligro la relación comercial de la competición con el gigante asiático
articles.body: Todo lo que se está viviendo entre LaLiga, el Real Madrid, Kylian Mbappé y China ya le sucedió a la NBA en 2019. Esta vez ha sido por un mensaje del delantero blanco refiriéndose al meme que circula por las redes sociales en las que aparece su cara como si fuera Mao Zedong. Hace siete años, fue por una frase de apenas seis palabras de Daryl Morey, en aquella época general manager de los Rockets, que desencadenó la mayor crisis internacional en la historia de la Liga estadounidense. El 4 de octubre de aquel año, Morey publicó en Twitter una imagen con el lema: "Fight for Freedom. Stand with Hong Kong". Apoyaba así a ese territorio autonómo chino, que por entonces vivía protestas en favor de la democracia. Las manifestaciones, iniciadas meses antes contra un proyecto de ley de extradición y convertidas después en un movimiento más amplio contra el gobierno de Pekín, habían generado una enorme tensión política. El mensaje del dirigente de los Rockets, equipo en el que precisamente militó Yao Ming, gran icono del baloncesto chino, chocó frontalmente con la posición de las autoridades chinas y con los intereses comerciales de la NBA. Hace años que la Liga se beneficia del amplio mercado de uno de los países más poblados del mundo, que en la actualidad tiene más de 1.400 millones de habitantes, sólo por detrás de India. La reacción fue inmediata. Morey borró el mensaje e intentó rebajar la tensión, asegurando que no pretendía ofender a los aficionados ni a los patrocinadores chinos y que había expresado una opinión personal. El propietario de los Rockets, Tilman Fertitta, se apresuró a desvincular a la franquicia de aquellas declaraciones y afirmó que el equipo no tenía una posición política. Sin embargo, las explicaciones no evitaron la tormenta. La Asociación China de Baloncesto, presidida entonces por el mencionado Yao Ming, suspendió su cooperación con Houston, mientras varias empresas y patrocinadores anunciaron la ruptura o paralización los acuerdos existentes. La NBA se encontró así atrapada entre la defensa de uno de sus directivos y la presión de un mercado de enorme valor económico. El conflicto adquirió una dimensión global cuando la televisión estatal china CCTV anunció que dejaría de emitir partidos de la NBA. Tencent, la plataforma digital que contaba con un importante acuerdo de retransmisión, también suspendió las emisiones de los encuentros de los Rockets, mientras otras compañías retiraban productos del equipo de sus tiendas. La polémica estalló, además, en vísperas de los partidos de pretemporada que debían disputar en China los Lakers y los Nets. Finalmente se acabaron celebrando, pero a costa de tener que cancelar numerosos actos publicitarios y de promoción. Aquella crisis mostró lo mismo que está sucediendo ahora con LaLiga, como una simple declaración individual, ya sea broma o mensaje serio, puede comprometer relaciones empresariales construidas durante años entre una competición deportiva y un país que es uno de los principales mercados de la misma. La respuesta de la propia NBA tampoco estuvo exenta de controversia. Lamentó que el mensaje de Morey hubiera ofendido a aficionados chinos, pero el comisionado Adam Silver defendió posteriormente el derecho del ejecutivo a expresar sus opiniones y dejó claro que ellos no debían ni podían controlar lo que sus empleados pensaban sobre cuestiones políticas. Aseguró también que la crisis no le costaría el cargo a Morey. Las consecuencias económicas se prolongaron mucho más allá de aquellas semanas. La NBA llegó a estimar que el deterioro de las relaciones con China podía costarle unos 400 millones de dólares. La paz llegó de forma gradual, sin que Morey tuviera que retractarse de su postura política. En octubre de 2020, CCTV volvió a emitir un partido de la NBA por primera vez desde el inicio del conflicto, al ofrecer el quinto encuentro de la final entre los Lakers y los Heat, disputado en la burbuja de Disney debido al coronavirus. La llegada hasta la normalidad, sin embargo, fue progresiva. La televisión estatal china no recuperó de forma más amplia las retransmisiones hasta marzo de 2022, cuando volvió a emitir un partido de la Liga tras aproximadamente 18 meses de ausencia. Hasta hace poco, 2025, la NBA no había recuperado todos sus contratos televisivos y de patrocinio en China. La crisis, eso sí, dejó una huella que todavía se recuerda con escalofríos en la Liga por todo lo que pudo perder.

articles.title: Blazers vs. Lakers Box Score Stats, Highlights for Luka, Ja, Dame, Reaves, Top Players
articles.summary: In a matchup of two undefeated teams, the Portland Trail Blazers defeated the Los Angeles Lakers 136-129 at Crypto.com Arena on Tuesday night.
articles.body:
In a matchup of two undefeated teams, the Portland Trail Blazers defeated the Los Angeles Lakers 136-129 at Crypto.com Arena on Tuesday night.

The Blazers moved to 3-0 thanks to Damian Lillard, Ja Morant, Jrue Holiday and Deni Avdija all scoring more than 20 points in a game for the first time this season.

Despite the loss, Luka Dončić recorded his second consecutive game with at least 40 points and better than 50 percent shooting from the field.

This was a matchup of the two best offensive teams in the NBA by rating to start the season. That certainly played out in this game with Dončić putting on another clinic, recording his third game with at least five made threes and showcasing his usual passing wizardry.

The first quarter, in particular, through four games has seen Dončić look virtually unstoppable. He dropped 16 points in the opening quarter to record his 20th game with at least 40 points since joining the Lakers.

Austin Reaves helped shoulder some of the offensive burden by recording his fourth straight game with at least 20 points and four assists.

This was only Dončić's 95th game with Los Angeles since the trade with the Dallas Mavericks. Anthony Edwards and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander are the only other players with at least 10 40-point games since that time.

Even with the Lakers' duo doing their part, it wasn't enough because the Blazers remain an unstoppable force right now. Any concerns about the fit between Lillard and Morant have proven to be unfounded thus far.

It doesn't hurt that Avdija is following up his breakout 2025-26 season with another strong start and Holiday has given their second unit a huge boost by coming off the bench.

Perhaps the most surprising part of the Blazers' start is they are currently third in defensive rating.

It's an incredibly small sample size, and their first two games were against the Phoenix Suns and Sacramento Kings, but if they can stay anywhere close to league average as the season moves on, there's more than enough talent on the offensive end of the floor for the Blazers to be a factor in the playoff race.

Given how many injuries have already occurred to key players on Western Conference contenders, the Blazers' outlook isn't too bad amid a 3-0 start.

The Lakers' issues on defense this game were to be expected because they aren't loaded with talent on that end of the floor, but the trio of Dončić, Reaves and Walker Kessler gives them such a high offensive ceiling that they can win a lot of games.

Next up for the Blazers is a home game against the Memphis Grizzlies on Thursday. The Lakers will play the second night of a back-to-back on Wednesday against the Los Angeles Clippers at the Intuit Dome.

articles.title: Ja Morant to Appeal Flopping Technical as Blazers HC Micah Nori Shades Refs After Win vs. Lakers
articles.summary: Portland Trail Blazers guard Ja Morant declared that he plans to appeal the technical foul he was assessed for flopping late in Tuesday night's 136-129 road win over the Los Angeles Lakers.
articles.body:
Portland Trail Blazers guard Ja Morant declared that he plans to appeal the technical foul he was assessed for flopping late in Tuesday night's 136-129 road win over the Los Angeles Lakers.

Regarding the call and why he intends on appealing, Morant told reporters , "I just showed my hands and took a bump in my chest. It ain't like I fell. I just kept going backwards. It is what it is. I'll try to appeal it. I think it's like a $2,000 [fine]."

The call was made with 3:49 remaining in regulation when Lakers guard Austin Reaves attempted to drive to the basket. Morant absorbed contact and stumbled backward on the play.

It was one of three flopping calls made against Portland in the final six minutes of the game, which Blazers head coach Micah Nori flagged as strange since there were only "27 flops called last year in 2,000 games total."

Nori also told reporters , "Good job by the NBA. Point of emphasis. Great job. There were [71] free throws. We almost got past 2 a.m. on the East Coast for the [end of the] game. Sorry to keep you all here so long."

Despite the controversial calls, Portland persevered and remained one of just four undefeated teams in the NBA by improving to 3-0. Meanwhile, the Lakers suffered their first loss, falling to 3-1.

The Blazers got contributions up and down the lineup, as six players scored in double figures and four topped 20 points, led by Morant's 23.

Lakers superstar guard Luka Dončić went off for a game-high 41 points, and Reaves added 26, but Portland's balanced attack ultimately won the night.

articles.title: Ja Morant mocked by NBA official Scott Foster while arguing against technical foul call
articles.summary: Ja Morant said he would appeal a possible fine.
articles.body:
The NBA decided to make flopping a point of emphasis this season, and no officiating crew heard that message louder than the one that presided over the Portland Trail Blazers' 136-129 win over the Los Angeles Lakers on Tuesday. Three flopping fouls were called at the end of the contest, each of which had the potential to swing the game.

One of those fouls was called on Trail Blazers guard Ja Morant, who was spotted on the broadcast trying to plead his case to NBA official Scott Foster. After hearing Morant out for a bit, Foster animatedly imitated Morant's flop to show the guard what the officials saw.

Morant continued to argue his case briefly before Foster walked away.

After the contest, Morant said he planned to appeal the call , as he does not want to get fined, per ESPN.

"It ain't like I fell. I just kept going backwards. It is what it is. I'll try to appeal it. I think it's like a $2,000 [fine]."

Morant added that the Trail Blazers did switch up their defensive approach late in the game in an attempt to show officials the Lakers were initiating contact. In that one example, however, the officials determined Morant went too far in trying to sell that contact.

Trail Blazers head coach Micah Nori seemed to agree that the officials were way too happy to call flopping fouls at the end of the game. During his postgame presser, Nori playfully teased the league for making flopping fouls a point of emphasis this season, per ESPN.

"Good job by the NBA," Nori said. "Point of emphasis. Great job. There were [71] free throws. We almost got past 2 a.m. on the East Coast for the [end of the] game. Sorry to keep you all here so long."

While comments like that have resulted in fines in the past, Nori wasn't angry when he said it. He matter-of-factly stated that the NBA followed through on its promise. Because of that, it's unclear if his light criticism will draw attention from the league.

In September, the NBA announced it would crack down on flopping during the 2026-27 season. At the time, the NBA's head of referee development and training, Monty McCutchen, said the league wanted to make sure the "game is played on its merits, not the theatrics of the merits."

Morant can confirm the officials have followed through on that promise thus far.

articles.title: El novato que se tira hasta las zapatillas
articles.standfirst: Darius Acuff Jr., combo de los Kings, está lanzando 23,3 veces por encuentro y se codea en la estadística con las grandes estrellas de la NBA: sólo Anthony Edwards tira más que él
articles.summary: Darius Acuff Jr., combo de los Kings, está lanzando 23,3 veces por encuentro y se codea en la estadística con las grandes estrellas de la NBA: sólo Anthony Edwards tira más que él
articles.body: Uno acude a las estadísticas de la NBA y compueba que los jugadores que más lanzamientos realizan por partido son, como casi siempre, algunas de las grandes estrellas de la competición: Anthony Edwards, Luka Doncic, Jayson Tatum, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Jalen Brunson... Aspirantes al MVP o a estar en los mejores quintetos de la temporada entre los que se cuela un nombre: Darius Acuff Jr., un novato que en los cuatro primeros partidos de su carrera profesional se ha tirado hasta las zapatillas. El combo de los Kings, de 1,88 metros y 19 años, es segundo en la estadística sólo por detrás del ahora lesionado Anthony Edwards. Hace nada menos que con 23,3 tiros por encuentro. Su acumulado de 93 lanzamientos de campo en los primeros cuatro partidos en la NBA encuentra pocas comparaciones. Wilt Chamberlain llegó a los 137. John Drew, a los 106. Y Kevin Durant, uno de los mejores anotadores puros de todos los tiempos, se quedó en 86. Acuff estuvo un solo año en la Universidad de Arkansas. Allí promedió 16,5 tiros por partido para tener una media de 23,5 puntos con un destacable 44,0% en triples. Con esa fama de anotador compulsivo le draftearon los Kings en el séptimo lugar del último draft. De momento, está tirando mucho, aunque sus porcentajes están dejando bastante que desear. Sus 93 tiros se han convertido en sólo 86 puntos. Promedia 21,5, pero con un 34,4% en tiros de campo y un 20,6% en triples. Hasta esta madrugada, que mejoró con 3/7, era el peor triplista de la NBA acumulando un 4/27. "Estoy fallando tiros que meto a diario. Ya vendrán", dice Acuff con confianza. Eso, confianza, es algo de lo que ha dado muestra de ir sobrado. En su debut en la NBA ante los Clippers acabó con 5/24 en tiros, incluido un 0/7 en triples. Llamó la atención su perseverancia pese a que estaba claro que no era su noche. "Es un inconsciente. Se la jugó cada vez. Nunca he visto a un novato así, tirando tantas veces en su debut", comentó el exjugador Jeff Teague, con 826 partidos NBA a sus espaldas y 12 años de experiencia. Lejos de arrugarse, en su segunda noche, frente a los Blazers, se fue a los 26 tiros. Metió 33 puntos, lo que hasta ahora es su tope. En ninguno de los cuatro partidos de los Kings hasta ahora, todo derrotas, por cierto, ha bajado de los 20 lanzamientos de campo. Tiene pinta de que en el individualista juego de Sacramento, va a poder seguir así. Pero eso tiene sus problemas. Draymond Green ya le advirtió durante un partido de pretemporada ante los Warriors. Aprovechando un parón, se dirigió a su joven rival. "Oye, amigo, ¿quién más tocó el balón en esa posesión?", le preguntó. "Nadie", respondió Acuff. Y comenzó una perorata del veterano en la que hablaba al novato sobre mantener a todos los compañeros metidos en el juego. "Puedes hacer que los chicos empiecen a tramar contra ti, chicos que realmente no quieren verte triunfar, chicos que empiezan a quejarse por ahí... Cuando vi eso, sólo quise darle un pequeño consejo", contó Green. "Me estaba diciendo que lea un poco más el juego... Trataba de enseñarme y yo estaba escuchando. Estaba de acuerdo con él", dijo el rookie, al que aún le falta poner en práctica la recomendación.
