articles.title: 76 college basketball predictions: Who will surprise, who will disappoint and who will win it all
articles.summary: To celebrate the start of the men's college basketball season, here are 76 predictions sure to come true (unless they don't).
articles.body:
The men's college basketball season tips off Sunday in Rome, Italy, when Villanova faces Notre Dame in a matchup pitting Pope Leo XIV's alma mater against a fellow Catholic power. To celebrate the start of the new season, here are 68 76 predictions sure to come true (unless they don't).

1. This will be college basketball's year of the asterisk. For months, opportunistic coaches have challenged the NCAA's ability to enforce its own eligibility rules in court by targeting players who don't fit the traditional college model — overseas pros, G league veterans, players once thought to have exhausted their college eligibility. Programs in the hunt for the national title will face questions about the fairness of the race and the legitimacy of their rosters. The team that cuts down the nets may be the one that navigates the legal system best.

2. Team whose outlook depends most on the outcome of eligibility battles with the NCAA: Kansas. Bill Self bolstered an underwhelming roster by adding three projected starters in the past month, including 24-year-old sixth-year senior Trey Kaufman-Renn, a second-round draft pick of the Minnesota Timberwolves this past June. The Jayhawks would vault from fringe Top 25 team to national title contender if Kaufman-Renn, Melvin Council, 24, and Tre White, 23, all win their legal fights for an extra season of eligibility.

3. Most impactful ACC eligibility cases: Seth Trimble (Louisville), Malik Reneau (Miami)

4. Most impactful Big East eligibility cases: Keyshawn Hall and Babacar Sane (St. John's), Filip Borovicanin (Xavier), Vince Iwuchukwu (Georgetown)

5. Most impactful Big Ten eligibility cases: Roddy Gayle (Michigan), Cade Tyson (Minnesota)

6. Most impactful Big 12 eligibility cases: Tamin Lipsey (Iowa State), RJ Godfrey (Arizona), Jaxon Kohler (BYU), Darrion Williams and Jamichael Stillwell (Texas Tech), MJ Collins (Cincinnati), Council, White and Kaufman-Renn (Kansas)

7. Most impactful SEC eligibility cases: Donovan Dent and Skyy Clark (LSU), Denzel Aberdeen (Florida), Mark Mitchell (Missouri)

8. Other eligibility cases that matter: Robbie Avila (Saint Louis), Xaivian Lee and Javon Bennett (Gonzaga), Jaden Henley (Grand Canyon)

9. The legal wrangling won't stop once the regular season begins. Expect fifth-year players to gain or lose eligibility throughout the winter as litigation progresses or appeals are heard. And expect teams to try to plug roster holes with players facing eligibility questions at the semester break.

10. Team outside the AP preseason Top 25 who could surprise: Indiana. Only two rotation players return from the team that won a modest 18 games in Darren DeVries' debut season, but Indiana has reloaded via a spending spree in the transfer portal. Between Markus Burton's creativity off the dribble, Aiden Sherrell's combination of size and skill and a deep supporting cast, the Hoosiers have second-weekend NCAA tournament potential.

11. Preseason Top 25 team who could disappoint: USC. The Trojans are loaded with individual talent, but the pieces don't seem to fit together in a way that makes sense. Will Eric Musselman be able to define roles and get players to sacrifice when so many are used to having the ball in their hands? The other concern is the status of two key players. Promising 7-foot UConn transfer Eric Reibe has yet to play after undergoing offseason foot surgery, nor has top recruit Christian Collins for undisclosed reasons.

12. Reigning national champion Michigan can still challenge for a top-four Big Ten finish even after losing head coach Dusty May and three lottery picks from last season — and then losing top recruit Brandon McCoy to a season-ending knee injury in late August. Elliot Cadeau is a top-five point guard in college basketball, Trey McKenney is an obvious breakout candidate and the frontcourt handpicked by May out of the transfer portal is intriguing. This is still a very good roster, just not a historically great one.

13. Football schools that will have more success on the hardwood this season : Florida, Michigan, USC

14. Basketball schools that will have more success on the gridiron this season: Indiana, UCLA, Wake Forest

15. School that will be putrid in both: Sorry, Penn State.

16. The NCAA tournament expansion that no one asked for will still be wildly unpopular after the inaugural edition. Expanding the field from 68 teams to 76 damages sporting perfection so that the power conferences can gain a little extra TV money and send a few more middling teams to March Madness. If anything, 68 was four teams too many.

17. The biggest complaint will be that 76 teams further devalues college basketball's regular season by lowering the bar for power-conference teams to earn a NCAA tournament berth and reducing the consequences of losses. Get ready for a field that includes multiple 15-loss teams from power conferences and for the 11th-place teams from the SEC and Big Ten to make it in with ease.

18. If you ignored the First Four — and most of you did — you'll continue to ignore the new play-in games. Most bracket challenges organized by major media outlets will still begin the Thursday morning after Selection Sunday when the field has shrunk to 64 teams. That's when the mainstream audience will tune in.

19. The opening Thursday and Friday of the NCAA tournament will remain pseudo national holidays. Try as they might, Greg Sankey and fellow greedy power-conference commissioners can't mess that up.

20. Mark Pope needs better results to remain at Kentucky. In his first two seasons as head coach at Kentucky, Pope has not finished higher than sixth in the SEC, nor has he advanced beyond the Sweet 16. At least one of those two things must change for Pope to keep his job beyond this season. Tradition-rich Kentucky is spending too much on its roster to have patience much longer

21. The addition of prized Iowa State transfer Milan Momcilovich gives Pope hope of the type of confidence-boosting season he needs to restore faith . The 6-foot-9 stretch forward made 48.6% of his 280 3-point attempts last season with the Cyclones. Pope needs Momcilovich to pick up where he left off and a couple of the talented but unproven players around him — Malachi Moreno? Alex Wilkins? Kam Williams? — to produce breakout seasons.

22. Exhibition losses that could be a sign of things to come: Xavier 86, Tennessee 70 and Duke 103, Tennessee 64. Two dreadful performances in a span of five days have Vols fans questioning whether this team can live up to the standard Rick Barnes has set. Barnes may eventually unlock the potential of a decorated transfer class, find a capable interior presence and coax his team into defending and rebounding, but right now Tennessee is nowhere close to the eighth best team in America.

23. Exhibition losses that are more fluke than omen: UConn 78, Michigan State 70 and Marquette 86, Michigan State 79. The center position, as Dan Hurley so bluntly pointed out, is an issue for the Spartans , especially with newcomer Anton Bonke failing to inspire confidence in his debut. Still, the Spartans' perimeter corps is loaded and point guard Jeremy Fears will play better than he did in these games.

24. He may only be 17 years old, but Duke's Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje is going to make a panel of media voters look silly for not including him on the preseason all-ACC first team — and barely finding room for him on the second team! The potential No. 1 pick in the 2028 NBA Draft is an unusually skilled 7-footer who excels at knocking down threes, facilitating from the high post or defending multiple positions. He was the MVP of the gold medal-winning U.S. team at this past summer's U-17 World Championships.

25. Dan Hurley will continue to fool opposing fans into thinking he's a jerk when in reality he just plays one on TV. Behind the sideline antics and ref berating is a good-hearted, thoughtful, self-aware coach whose players swear by him.

26. It used to be that newly hired coaches could count on administrators giving them four-plus years to turn around struggling programs. Not anymore. The transfer portal has made it possible to revitalize a talent-bereft roster in a single offseason. As a result, more coaches will lose their jobs after just two or three seasons if they aren't showing progress. Just look at last year's cycle, when Providence ousted onetime rising star Kim English after just three seasons and Syracuse did the same with alum Adrian Autry.

27. The coach under the most pressure to win to save his job this year is Pittsburgh's Jeff Capel. After Capel's Panthers lost 20 games and missed the NCAA tournament for the seventh time in his up-and-down eight seasons, athletic director Allen Greene had to announce that Capel would return for a ninth campaign — never a good sign for a coach's future. The Panthers landed an intriguing 11-man transfer class highlighted by Baye Ndongo and former McDonald's All-American Jalil Bethea, but they were projected to finish just 13th in the ACC preseason poll. Capel will need to exceed that to keep donors from raising money to pay for his buyout.

28. Other coaches whose jobs will be in jeopardy if they don't win this season: Memphis' Penny Hardaway, Kentucky's Mark Pope, South Carolina's Lamont Paris, Wake Forest's Steve Forbes, Washington's Danny Sprinkle, Penn State's Mike Rhoades

29. Coaches facing prove-it seasons as they try to earn the full-time gig: Oregon interim coach Tony Stubblefield and Michigan's Mike Boynton, who formally shed the interim label when he received a two-year contract in July.

30. Will Wade will keep testing the NCAA's ability to enforce its own rules as he essentially tries to assemble a professional roster to play college basketball. This offseason, Wade targeted 23-and-over college players seeking a fifth season of eligibility and 23-and-over overseas pros who have played in some of the top leagues around the world. He even explored the possibility of rostering former St. John's standout RJ Luis, who entered the 2025 NBA Draft after his junior season and signed two-way contracts with the Utah Jazz and Boston Celtics.

31. There's a reason LeBron James has laughed at the idea of delaying retirement long enough to wait for his younger son to join him in the NBA. Arizona sophomore Bryce James still has a long road ahead of him as he tries to develop into an NBA prospect in the 3-and-D wing archetype. After redshirting as a freshman, James is likely to crack Arizona's rotation as a sophomore, particularly if Godfrey is not ruled eligible. The 6-foot-5 sophomore started all three of Arizona's exhibition games but played no more than 15 minutes in any of them. He tallied a combined six points and zero rebounds.

32. ACC breakout star: Chance Mallory, G, Virginia

33. Big East breakout star: Jayden Ross, F, UConn

34. Big Ten breakout star: Trey McKenney, G, Michigan

35. Big 12 breakout star: Chase McCarty, F, Houston

36. SEC breakout star: Malachi Moreno, C, Kentucky

37. NBA teams may not be as tempted as usual to tank this season in hopes of securing a top pick in the 2027 draft. And not because of a change in the rules. There are no surefire can't-miss stars in this year's freshman class, no AJ Dybantsas or Darryn Petersons, no Caleb Wilsons or Cameron Boozers.

38. Kansas freshman Tyran Stokes is the only player with physical tools comparable to the top players from last year's class, but scouts question the long, athletic 6-foot-7 wing's emotional maturity and turnover-prone decision making. Stokes took a step toward solidifying himself as the future No. 1 overall pick in an exhibition loss to Duke this past Sunday. He drew a game-high nine fouls over the course of a 27-point, 8-rebound, 7-assist performance.

39. Freshmen besides Stokes who will make the biggest impact this season: Jordan Smith Jr. (Arkansas), Caleb Holt (Arizona), Jason Crowe Jr. (Missouri)

40. Freshmen ranked outside the Rivals top 15 who will make the biggest impact this season: Miles Sadler (West Virginia), Obinna Ekezie Jr. (Louisville), Quentin Coleman (Illinois)

41. Trend that will have staying power: Freshmen ranked in the top 150 committing to mid-majors despite interest from power-conference programs. Pepperdine, UC Irvine, VCU, Florida Atlantic, Florida International, Utah Tech, Liberty and George Mason each landed at least one such player. With more top programs preferring to rely on veterans, these freshmen are making a shrewd choice gambling that they can parlay 1-2 dominant seasons at the mid-major level into the chance to transfer up to a power conference program for a massive payday.

42. Arizona will have three first-round picks in next year's draft, maybe even three lottery picks if highly touted freshman Caleb Holt progresses as a playmaker and wing Ivan Kharchenkov and 7-footer Motiejus Krivas evolve from defense-first role players to two-way contributors.

43. What will determine if Arizona emerges as a true tier-one title contender is the supporting cast. Can transfers Derek Dixon and JJ Mandaquit emerge as a formidable combination at point guard? Will fifth-year transfer RJ Godfrey win his eligibility battle? And, if not, who will fill the void at power forward created by Koa Peat bolting for the NBA?

44. It's time to re-evaluate Baylor after the Bears delivered back-to-back exhibition victories against two of the top three teams in the AP Top 25. Yes, they were only exhibitions, but beating Florida and Illinois was majorly impressive. Baylor did not receive a single vote in the preseason AP Top 25 and was projected to finish 10th in the Big 12. Scott Drew's Bears have a chance to make both those look silly very quickly.

45. Midnight is likely to come early again for Cinderella this March. Two years ago, no team from outside the power conferences advanced to the round of 16 for the first time since the NCAA tournament expanded to 64 teams in 1985. Last year, it happened again . Talent is concentrating at the power-conference level like never before because top-tier programs can offer massive NIL payouts to the best available players and because transfer rules no longer prevent players from switching schools as often as they want without penalty.

46. That said, don't be surprised if one or two small-conference underdogs still spring early-round upsets. Last year, Santa Clara nearly toppled Kentucky, Siena led top-seeded Duke deep into the second half and Wright State pushed Virginia. If a couple of those close games go the other way, the conversation would have been different.

47. Mid-major who could string together a couple wins this March: High Point. This could be the strongest High Point team yet, better even than last year's edition that won 31 games and took down Wisconsin in the opening round of the NCAA tournament. The well-funded Panthers have reloaded thanks to the return of Big South preseason player of the year Cam'ron Fletcher and the arrival of a decorated group of transfers.

48. Other mid-majors who will be dangerous: Grand Canyon, Saint Louis, New Mexico, VCU, Utah State, Santa Clara, McNeese, Wichita State.

49. At least 11 SEC teams will make the NCAA tournament — and 12 or 13 is not out of the realm of possibility. Deep-pocketed SEC programs have spent big to retain elite talent and load up on proven transfers and coveted newcomers. This will be the top league in college basketball again, just like it was two years ago.

50. Texas isn't just the SEC team most likely to dethrone preseason No. 1 Florida as league champs. The Longhorns are talented enough for Sean Miller to finally shed the label of college basketball's best coach never to make a Final Four. The frontcourt is so loaded that decorated freshman Marcus Spears Jr. is likely to start the season coming off the bench behind preseason second-team all-SEC center Matas Vokietaitis and high-motor TCU transfer David Punch. And the perimeter corps aren't bad either, headlined by point guard Isaiah Johnson, a prized transfer from Colorado.

51. Alabama coach Nate Oats isn't someone who would shy away from bringing in players with dubious eligibility cases, so the fact that the Tide didn't make any late additions this summer is probably a sign that he likes his roster. Will the backcourt of Aden Holloway and Amari Allen help Alabama outperform its preseason No. 20 ranking and finish in the top four in the SEC? The guess here is yes.

52. Incoming international players who will make the biggest impact this season: Quinn Ellis (St. John's), Saliou Niang (LSU), Nikola Kusturica (UCLA)

53. Is this Bill Self's final season at Kansas? The question will hang over the Jayhawks until Self confirms that he's coming back for another year or retiring after the NCAA tournament. Self has dealt with a flurry of health issues the past few years. Not even he probably knows for sure yet if this season is his finale.

54. Top ACC transfer: Flory Bidunga (Kansas to Louisville)

55. Top Big East transfer: Tounde Yessoufou (Baylor to St. John's)

56. Top Big Ten transfer: Markus Burton (Notre Dame to Indiana)

57. Top Big 12 transfer: Darrion Williams (NC State to Texas Tech)

58. Top Pac-12 transfer: Massamba Diop (Arizona State to Gonzaga)

59. Top SEC transfer: Milan Momcilovich (Iowa State to Kentucky)

60. This year's Maui Invitational will be an improvement over last year's abomination but it still won't be must-see Thanksgiving week TV like previous iterations. Preseason No. 5 Arizona is the only headliner. BYU, VCU, Providence, Ole Miss, Clemson, Colorado State and Washington round out a solid but unremarkable field.

61. Expect the Maui Invitational to continue to fade from relevance unless organizers find a way to compete with the 24-team Players Era Festival, which grants each program that participates $1 million for NIL allocation. This year's Players Era tournaments include many of the top programs in college basketball. Meanwhile, check out the underwhelming 2027 Maui field.

62. Team that will make the biggest leap this season: Marquette. After enduring a nightmarish 20-loss season last winter, Shaka Smart has the Golden Eagles poised to return to the NCAA tournament. Sophomore point guard Nigel James Jr. headlines a list of nine returners, providing more continuity than almost every other program in the country. And after going four years without taking a transfer, Smart finally dipped into the portal again, adding Louisville center Sananda Fru and St. Thomas guard Nolan Minessale.

63. Team that will fall the farthest this season: Purdue. This could look like a terrible call by Christmas — I know, I know, always bet on Matt Painter — but the Boilermakers have to replace four starters, including the NCAA's all-time assists leader. The returning players will have to take on expanded roles while adjusting to a drastic stylistic change without a true back-to-the-basket threat for the first time in years.

64. New North Carolina coach Michael Malone will have to validate his reputation for X's-and-O's wizardry to catapult the Tar Heels to national relevance during his inaugural season. This revamped, newcomer-laden roster appears more fringe Top 25-worthy than one capable of challenging Duke for ACC supremacy.

65. Coach who will be in most demand next spring: Josh Schertz, Saint Louis. He was already a candidate for several high-major openings last spring after guiding the Billikens to 29 wins in just his second season with the program. Now, Schertz has another roster capable of winning the Atlantic 10 and breaking into the AP Top 25, so expect him to have his pick of multiple jobs once again next year.

66. Other coaches in position to move up: Eric Olen (New Mexico), Flynn Clayman (High Point), Phil Martelli Jr. (VCU)

67. Division I players whose names will receive the most attention during TV broadcasts next season: Vanderbilt forward Chandler Bing, Loyola Marymount guard All Wright and UT Rio Grande Valley guard Always Wright.

68. None of them can claim the sport's most eye-catching name. Meet Amillion Buggs of Division II West Alabama.

69. Ben McCollum has a long history of finding a way to win without departed stars, so expect Iowa to exceed expectations despite the loss of Bennett Stirtz. A half-dozen rotation players return for the Hawkeyes, but Stirtz was the player who generated open shots for himself and his teammates. For Iowa to be good again, McCollum will need to develop another leverage player who can create advantages.

70. Decision to stay in school that will look smart: Thomas Haugh, Florida. He likely would have been a first-round pick had he entered the 2026 NBA Draft, but Haugh instead agreed to return to Florida on an NIL deal that reportedly will exceed $8 million . That means Haugh is making more than he would have as an NBA rookie while chasing a second championship at Florida and potentially boosting his draft stock even higher.

71. Projected national coach of the year: Jai Lucas, Miami

72. Projected national player of the year: Thomas Haugh, Florida

73. Projected first-team All-Americans: Jeremy Fears, G, Michigan State; Tyler Tanner, G, Vanderbilt; Thomas Haugh, F, Florida; David Mirkovic, F, Illinois; Motiejus Krivas, C, Arizona

74. Early Final Four prediction: Duke, Florida, Texas, UConn

75. Early national champion prediction: Duke

76. Most of these preseason predictions will probably be wrong. The most fun part of college basketball is that it always defies expectations.

articles.title: If the Valkyries win the WNBA Finals, who should win Finals MVP?
articles.summary: With the Valkyries one win away, let's look at the cases for the top candidates if they're able to pull this off.
articles.body:
After a 64-55 defensive slugfest in Game 5 on Monday night, the Golden State Valkyries find themselves on the cusp of their first championship. Their defense led the dance, as it has all year, forcing the Dream into yet another low-efficiency, high-turnover contest.

They're on the cusp of not just winning a championship, but putting a bow on one of the most impressive franchise sprints we've seen in sports history. Two cracks at one win, paying off a promise from Valkyries owner Joe Lacob that the team would win a championship within its first five years — with three to spare .

Expansion teams aren't supposed to have success this early, but the Natalie Nakase-led group made the playoffs — behind a strong defense, of course — in their inaugural season. They've now followed up that campaign with a top-two standings finish — while having a historically great defense and leading the WNBA in net rating (+9.1) — and two impressive series wins over the Dallas Wings and Las Vegas Aces.

But of course, three more words: job's not finished.

They still have to finish their dinner. It's not like the Dream are incapable of bouncing back and stringing together wins; we're roughly a week removed from the Dream countering a Game 1 loss by reeling off two straight impressive victories.

With the Valkyries one win away, though, it's natural to look ahead to what that means on the individual side. Finals MVP is generally an easy checklist:

If not, are you at least your team's top decision-maker?

Were you at least serviceable defensively?

Just go down the list of Finals MVP winners over the past 10 years: A'ja Wilson (x2), Jonquel Jones, Chelsea Gray, Kahleah Copper, Breanna Stewart (x2), Emma Meesseman, Sylvia Fowles and Candace Parker. Every last one of them fit into at least two, if not three of those points.

The #StrengthInNumbers vibe of this Valkyries group makes this a more interesting conversation to sort through. As such, let's talk through the cases of who I believe to be their top-3 options if they're able to pull this off.

Stats: 5.6 points (69/38/50 splits; 64 true shooting), 10.6 rebounds (3 OREB), 3.4 blocks

For a series that has undoubtedly been defined by defense, Stokes' defense has stood out this entire series. It would be easy to point to the blocks; she's not only leading the Finals in blocks per game, but she now has the record for most blocks in a Finals series.

She has been the lone consistent answer to the Angel Reese Experience in this series. While Reese has been able to win matchups against Kayla Thornton, Laeticia Amihere, Aminata Gueye and others, she hasn't had an answer for Stokes. Reese was a ghastly 5-of-21 on shots contested by Stokes after Game 4 ; you can add Game 5's 0-for-3 count to the tally now.

The rim protection and shot deterrence has been there. The rebounding has been stout, on both ends of the floor. There's been little success from the Dream when they've attempted to run a pick-and-roll in Stokes' direction.

As timely and impactful as Stokes' 13-point surge in Game 5 was, the flip side of that is Stokes having 15 points in the series entering Game 5. History wouldn't be on her side: Detroit Shock center Ruth Riley's 14.7 points per game in 2003 is the lowest average we've seen from a Finals MVP winner.

Stokes isn't tasked with a heavy scoring load, and she does provide value as a screener (on and off the ball) and mid-possession connector with handoffs, but it's fair to note the lack of scoring prowess and scouting report equity compared to Gabby Williams or Veronica Burton.

The other thing that hurts her case, at least statistically: the Valkyries have lost her minutes in the series so far (-16 in 147 minutes), something you can't say for Burton (+4 in 159 minutes) or Williams (neutral in 167 minutes).

Stats: 9 points (31/26/78 splits; 38.2 true shooting), 4.8 rebounds, 3.4 assists, 1.6 steals, 2 blocks

She's spent most of the series making life miserable for Jordin Canada; per Synergy tracking data, Canada is a whopping 6-of-24 (25% FG) on shots defended by Burton. There have been spells where she's been moved around the board, notably taking the Rhyne Howard assignment in Game 3.

Beyond the on-ball stuff, Burton has been phenomenal as an off-ball defender. There's still the navigation that comes with tracking Atlanta's pindowns and staggers, but she's provided real juice as a rim protector. She has consistently nailed her low-man responsibilities when put in that spot, culminating in a four-block explosion in Game 5 — one that put her name next to the legendary Diana Taurasi as the only guards in Finals history to log four blocks in a Finals game.

On the other end, Burton hasn't been at her usual level (more on that shortly), but she's been a timely shot-maker in Golden State's three wins. Her drives, and the playmaking tied to those drives, have also been important as they've searched for answers to Atlanta's excellent defense.

To put it plainly: Burton simply has not scored enough or done so efficiently enough.

While the driving volume perking up has been a welcome development, she hasn't had a consistent dose of finishing or foul-drawing (1.8 free throw attempts per game) to really put a stamp on her case. Add in porous 3-point shooting (with relatively low volume), and you kinda have to ding her for that.

Stats: 16.2 points (35/20/88 splits; 40.1 true shooting), 3.8 rebounds, 3.2 assists, 2.6 steals

It's a straightforward case to make: she's both at the top of the scouting report for the Dream, while largely being tasked with defending the Dream's best perimeter player (Howard) in the process.

Williams leads both teams in scoring (16.2), is second only to Howard in fourth-quarter scoring (23), and it's hard to overstate just how stout Williams has been defensively. Her off-ball work in particular has been superb, a big reason why she's leading the Finals in steals (2.6) and almost assuredly leading everyone in deflections if that was tracked anywhere publicly.

She doesn't have an easy job on either end of the floor, and she's handling that burden while operating at less than 100%.

(To Williams' credit, she has been asked about her knee — and, in general, how she's doing — multiple times throughout the series and she's practically shut down any talks that she's hurt. We also have eyes and know how competitive these players are. They won't be giving an inch.)

Voters will have to weigh Williams' two-way responsibility — and the fact she likely isn't 100% — with the fact she's converted 35% of her 2s and 20% of her 3s in the process. It's been an isolation-heavy series for Williams, mostly out of necessity, but the efficiency simply hasn't been there to this point.

articles.title: New Warriors Rumors on Kristaps Porzinigis, 'Extreme Level of Pessimism' of Return amid Trade Buzz
articles.summary: The Golden State Warriors appear to be operating as if Kristaps Porziņģis will not play for them again due to his ongoing health issues.
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors appear to be operating as if Kristaps Porziņģis will not play for them again due to his ongoing health issues.

Per ESPN's Anthony Slater , people in the Warriors organization have expressed an "extreme level of pessimism" about Porziņģis ever suiting up for them again as they explore potential trades for the 31-year-old:

"Team sources continue to express an extreme level of pessimism that Porzingis will ever play for the Warriors again, but he could end up helping the organization in another way, because his contract, which is only guaranteed for $3 million next season, could still prove to be valuable in executing a trade."

Porziņģis Trade Idea Best For Warriors 💡

Steph, Dray Talk End of Dubs Partnership 🥺

The Warriors announced on Oct. 14 that Porziņģis would remain out indefinitely due to a "health-related matter" after a meeting with general manager Mike Dunleavy Jr. and vice president of player health and performance Dr. Rick Celebrini.

Porziņģis wrote on social media that same day he was still working with doctors and medical experts to "figure out how to be fully back to good health ASAP" and he was "getting better and better."

There was no indication in Porziņģis' statement about a potential return to basketball.

On Oct. 21, ESPN's Shams Charania reported the Warriors have "started exploring trade routes" for Porziņģis, who was "seriously contemplating his future in basketball" due to his health.

Porziņģis signed a two-year, $40 million deal with the Warriors during the offseason. He is making $20 million this season with a $20 million player option for 2027-28.

The option year for Porziņģis is only partially guaranteed for $3 million until July 7, 2027.

Slater noted the Warriors could look to use Porziņģis' "unwillingness to be present" at their facilities as a "a failure to render his services" in order to potentially void his contract.

Porziņģis was acquired by Golden State in a trade with the Atlanta Hawks prior to the in-season deadline last February. He appeared in 15 games for the Warriors, averaging 16.1 points and 5.3 rebounds.

articles.title: Paul Pierce: de ganar 198 millones de dólares, al borde de la bancarrota
articles.standfirst: La leyenda de los Celtics dice no poder afrontar la manutención de su exmujer y sus hijos
articles.summary: La leyenda de los Celtics dice no poder afrontar la manutención de su exmujer y sus hijos
articles.body: De manera recurrente, el universo NBA se sorprende (cada vez menos) con una antigua estrella que está al borde de la ruina o en bancarrota. Malas decisiones económicas, inversiones ruinosas, manutenciones de hijos y exexposas, no saber bajar el tren vida tras la retirada... El último caso es el de Paul Pierce, icono de los Celtics de finales de los 90 y primera década del siglo XXI, ganador de un anillo en 2008 y MVP de aquella final. Pierce, de 49 años, además de por los Celtics, pasó por Nets, Wizards y Clippers y fue 10 veces All Star. Su camiseta con el dorsal 34 cuelga de lo alto del TD Garden de Boston junto a la de los grandes mitos de la franquicia más laureada de siempre. Durante su carrera ganó unos 198 millones de dólares en contratos de baloncesto, sin contar publicitarios, con un máximo de 19,7 millones en la temporada 2009-10. Sin embargo, toda aquella gloria y el dinero se han esfumado. Según documentos judiciales obtenidos por el medion 'TMZ', el miembro del Salón de la Fama del baloncesto afirma que sus ingresos se han desplomado desde que perdió su trabajo en la televisión con 'Fox Sports' y que tiene dificultades para cumplir con sus obligaciones financieras mensuales. Esos problemas han salido a la luz durante una disputa legal relacionada con la manutención de sus hijos y los honorarios de los abogados. Al parecer, Pierce recibió su último salario de Fox Sports el pasado mes de agosto. Ganaba unos 120.000 dólares al mes, pero desde que entonces no ha percibido nada. Sus ingresos actuales equivalen a cero. Por eso, el exjugador dice estar "ahogándose financieramente", aunque dice tener unos 300.000 dólares en cuentas bancarias y 3 millones de dólares en propiedades. Según ha declarado Pierce, paga aproximadamente 28.000 dólares al mes en concepto de manutención de los hijos y otros 20.000 en concepto de pensión alimenticia para su cónyuge. Además, dice tener otros gastos mensuales que ascienden a 48.000 dólares y entre los que se incluirían cuidado de niños, comidas fuera y servicios públicos. Tras retirarse en 2017, Pierce ejerció como analista para ESPN y después para Fox Sports. Sin embargo, el programa en el que aparecía fue cancelado en 2025 y sus ingresos se han visto muy reducidos. A la nada, asegura él. Al menos, ese es el argumento que expone ante la justicia para no satisfacer las peticiones económicas de su expareja.

articles.title: Houston Comets Tease New Uniform Reveal in Video Ahead of WNBA Return for 2027 Season
articles.summary: The Houston Comets teased their new branding as they plan for their return to the WNBA in 2027.
articles.body:
The Houston Comets teased their new branding as they plan for their return to the WNBA in 2027.

The team provided a glimpse on social media ahead of Thursday's full reveal:

Based on the short clip, the Comets may be leaning a bit on their original design.

During Houston's first run, WNBA jerseys all followed a broad template. The Comets logo and word mark at least helped them stand out a bit.

Of course, winning four titles also helps establish your brand identity. The Comets reeled off a four-peat from 1997-2000 thanks to the legendary trio of Cynthia Cooper, Sheryl Swoopes and Tina Thompson.

By 2004, however, Houston's fortunes began to shift dramatically. The team missed the playoffs that season. Within a few years, fan interest and attendance started to decline . The WNBA assumed ownership in 2008 and the organization was eliminated entirely.

It was an unbefitting end to the W's original dynasty.

The league is in a far different place now. Television ratings and attendances have increased across multiple years, and there will be 18 teams once the 2030 tips off.

Calls for a Comets rebirth organically began to grow, culminating in the announcement the Connecticut Sun would relocate to Houston.

The branding reveal falls on the same day as Game 6 of the WNBA Finals, but that's unlikely to dampen the enthusiasm of the fans who have eagerly awaited the Comets' revival.

articles.title: Stephen Curry, Draymond Green Sound Off on Potential End of Iconic Warriors Partnership
articles.summary: Golden State Warriors stars Stephen Curry and Draymond Green are well aware the clock might be ticking on their legendary run together, but neither is fixated on how things might end.
articles.body:
Golden State Warriors stars Stephen Curry and Draymond Green are well aware the clock might be ticking on their legendary run together, but neither is fixated on how things might end.

"You acknowledge that this will end at some point," Curry told The Athletic's Nick Friedell . "Of course, you have it in the back of your mind because you know that there aren't that many years ahead.

"But we're mature enough to know you can stay in the moment and just enjoy what we're doing, what we're trying to build and whatever happens, however it plays out, this is kind of inevitable. We're close to the end, and that's just part of it, so you can have it both ways. The thoughts of the end only make the urgency now more real and more motivating, if you will, because that's all we can control."

"We're not looking at it like that at all, man," he said "I think the obvious situation is it could be it for me. Who f--king cares if that's it nine months from now? Who f--king cares eight months from now?"

Klay Thompson's free agency in 2024 was a pivot point for the Warriors and their current era. They could've re-signed the five-time All-Star, thus giving him the role and salary he wanted . Thompson, Curry and Green all could've ridden off into the sunset together.

Instead, Golden State reasonably concluded letting him walk was better for its championship aspirations.

Thompson's value has declined in the three years since he left, further justifying the decision.

By doing that, however, general manager Mike Dunleavy Jr. made it clear he won't let emotion and sentiment drive his personnel moves. Having already broken up the Splash Brothers, he won't hesitate to move Green if the right deal arises.

Prior to the 2026 trade deadline, the five-time All-Star was linked to a blockbuster swap for Giannis Antetokounmpo.

Nobody has any misconceptions about the Warriors in their present state, either. It's only the first week, but a 1-3 start provides more evidence that this isn't a championship-caliber team.

Assuming that holds true for the remainder of the year, it could impact the futures of Curry and Green. Green is a free agent next summer, while Curry has a player option for 2028-29.

That kind of lingering uncertainty, especially when you've been with the same team for your entire career, might get to some players. Curry and Green have had this hanging over them for multiple years now, so that probably influences their overall perspective.

articles.title: How Spurs' chemistry contributed to Julian Champagnie's big night
articles.summary: The defending West champions are the NBA's most intact team, and their on-court harmony was on display big time in Tuesday's rout of Sacramento.
articles.body:
Julian Champagnie pointed to the Spurs' roster continuity as a factor in his impressive sharpshooting in Tuesday night's 130-103 pounding of the winless Sacramento Kings.

The fifth-year forward pumped in a season-high 26 points on the strength of 8 of 13 from 3-point range in 25 minutes off the bench.

"They do a good job of finding both of us when you're open," he said of his teammates feeding him and Victor Wembanyama, who finished with a season-best 29 points on 14 of 21 from the field.

"Over the past couple of years, we've grown the chemistry and grown the relationships," Champagnie added. "We all know where we want to be on the court. I think it's a product of that."

Indeed, general manager Brian Wright made sure the Spurs were the NBA's most intact team heading into 2026-27 after the young squad reached the NBA Finals last season.

From Wembanyama on down to No. 4 guard Jordan McLaughlin, they returned an average of 96.2% of last season's minutes, points, starts and win shares, according to rotogrinders.com.

"We wanted a lot of people to be back because of what we experienced last year," Spurs coach Mitch Johnson said.

Champagnie six 3-pointers in the second period tied a franchise record. His eight 3-pointers in the first half matched his own record set last New Year's Eve against New York when he finished with a club-record 11 3-pointers.

The Spurs' season-high 35 assists also underscored their on-court harmony. Four starters finished with five or more helpers, with Devin Vassell's season-high eight topping the chart.

"The thing that was good to see is our team did a good job of recognizing where he was once he got going," Johnson said. "We've had some time in the past four years where we've done a poor job of that. And not intentionally. I think we've grown in that aspect a little bit. Tonight was an example of that."

articles.title: Even with early Game 6 tipoff on Thursday, Valkyries are confident fans will find a way to watch
articles.summary: With the potential WNBA championship-clinching contest not being played in primetime Thursday, many Golden State Valkyries fans may have to skip work to watch a potentially historic day in women’s basketball.
articles.body: Shaunice Christmas-Miller and her wife, Kendall, have the flexibility in their jobs to work from home Thursday and watch Game 6 of the WNBA Finals despite the early tipoff on the West Coast. That doesn’t mean either is happy with the Golden State-Atlanta game starting at 9:30 a.m. PDT at State Farm Arena in Atlanta, several hours ahead of the Cavaliers-Hawks NBA game Thursday night. With the potential championship-clinching contest not being played in primetime, they know many other fans won’t be able to skip work and watch a potentially historic day in women’s basketball. Shaunice Christmas-Miller, who works in human resources, wishes everybody involved had considered the various options further in advance to avoid such last-minute scrambling. “They should have thought ahead for the whole seven-game series,” she said. “The women deserve primetime slots.” Several of the WNBA Finals games have drawn record ratings, showing how much interest there is in the league, this series and its athletes. The Valkyries have sold out every game since they began as an expansion franchise last year. “They would never make the men’s NBA final happen at 9:30 in the morning,” said Kendall Christmas-Miller, an accounting manager for a medical tech company. “I’m glad that they found accommodations but there’s still more work to be done when it comes to prioritizing women’s sports, especially when they’re performing at this level and getting the viewership.” Warriors coach Steve Kerr plans to tune in over breakfast. “We’ll have a day off that day, so, yeah, I’ll be watching,” he said. He will hardly be alone, according to Shaunice and Kendall. The couple from San Jose has attended every home playoff game this season at Chase Center — nicknamed “Ballhalla” for the raucous atmosphere created by Valkyries fans — and they believe the fan base will still show up Thursday. “Absolutely, they will definitely find a way,” Shaunice said. Other fans are frustrated, too “MOVE THE HAWKS GAME WOMEN = PRIME TIME” read one sign at the arena Monday night, when the Valkyries moved within a victory of a championship by beating the Dream 64-55. Others expressed their feelings on social media. Rapper Flavor Flav posted Tuesday: “Thursday is a paid holiday. Because Flavor Flav said so.” Included in his post was a photo of a note directed to bosses everywhere as a permission slip of sorts requesting excused absences for employees, signed by Flavor Flav with dual titles beneath his name — “The World’s Greatest Hype Man” and “Official Supporter of Women’s Sports.” Ole Miss women’s coach Yolett McPhee-McCuin sounded off. “I’d rather play anywhere else than have a 12:30 tip for a WNBA FINALS game man! Not a good look! For fans and for the players,” she posted on social media. “Just my 2cents that no one asked for.” Kendall Christmas-Miller said while the decision to start the game early is disappointing, “women’s sports fans are resilient and we’re going to keep pushing and keep finding a way to show up.” Valkyries focus on what they can control Golden State coach Natalie Nakase and her players have focused all along on what they can control, and this certainly isn’t one of those things. But there were some clever postgame offerings: “Call in sick, I recommend it,” point guard Veronica Burton cracked. “Yeah, right? Y’all know how to fake a cough, didn’t we all do that?” teammate Kiah Stokes added. Guard Kaila Charles has no doubt the Valkyries will adjust for the early tipoff. “I think it’s a good thing that we’re able to play in a bigger arena so that they can have more people come and support women’s basketball,” Charles said. Golden State hosting early morning watch party Valkyries co-owner Peter Guber walked into Chase Center on Monday unconcerned about the franchise’s devoted home crowd coming together when it matters most, despite the morning challenges such as commuter traffic to get into San Francisco for a watch party. Supporters have been invited to gather outside at Chase Center’s Thrive City viewing area beneath the big screen, which is 74 feet wide and 42 feet high. “Whatever they do, they come where the action is and this is the action,” Guber said, insisting Golden State’s faithful fans will all be “up and ready to go.” Nakase has made public pleas to the fan base before, and she did so again. “The beauty of Ballhalla, they’ll sacrifice,” she said. “They’re going to sacrifice. They’re going to open that app, they’re going to open their phone, they’re going to watch. I have no doubt that everyone who has been supporting us through this whole way — maybe we picked up fans within the Finals — everybody’s going to watch. ... That’s what we do on Golden State, we sacrifice for the betterment of our team. “So our fans, I ain’t worried about it, our fans are going to show up, show out, we play for them because they show up, show out. They don’t ever miss a beat.” And on Thursday, even over their morning coffee. “We’ve got the best fans in the league,” Burton said, “so I’m sure they’ll be supporting us, whatever time.”

articles.title: Atlanta Dream Blames WNBA After Must-Win Finals Game 6 Is Scheduled for Shockingly Early Start
articles.summary: The Atlanta Dream will be forced to play Game 6 of the WNBA Finals around lunchtime on the East Coast on Thursday, October 27, which fans of the opposing tea...
articles.body:
The Atlanta Dream will be forced to play Game 6 of the WNBA Finals around lunchtime on the East Coast on Thursday, October 27, which fans of the opposing team, the Golden State Valkyries , will be forced to watch in the morning — and the organization is blaming the league for the awkward timing.

The scheduling change was announced on Monday, because the Atlanta Hawks are scheduled to play at the State Farm Arena, which the Dream has made their home court during playoffs, that night. There were also conflicts for Game 3 and 4 because of a Sombr concert and another Hawks game, sparking the Dream to post an open letter to fans which was posted on X on Wednesday, October 28.

"First, thank you. Thank you for showing up, showing out, and supporting the Atlanta Dream. Thank you for your patience, your flexibility, and your willingness to navigate all the hurdles being placed in front of us. This postseason has asked a lot of our fans, our partners, our players, and our city," read the letter, signed by owners Larry and Robyn Gottesdiener , Suzanne Abair and Renee Montgomery .

"But ATL knows how to handle adversity. It's what we do. And once again, the city and our fans will fill the building. On a workday. On a school day. In the early afternoon. We do not take that support for granted," they added. "This incredible run by our players has also made something else abundantly clear: the Atlanta Dream has earned the right to be taken seriously ."

The letter went on to detail how the conflict arose.

"Two months ago, when the WNBA finalized playoff dates and times, we raised concerns that the W Finals schedule conflicted with NBA games at State Farm Arena. As we moved through the playoffs, we reiterated those concerns. Our concerns did not receive the attention, nor the urgency that they deserved," the owners wrote.

The Dream's home games this season were mostly played at the Gateway Center Arena, but it only has a capacity of 3,500, according to The Athletic , so the team was able to arrange for some playoff games at State Farm Arena, which will also become their home next season and has room for 17,000.

Per The Athletic , the WNBA sent a memo to all owners last December with "playoff hold dates" and asked them to secure all the dates for their home arena — Gateway Center, in the Dream's case — and if they couldn't, they were asked to explain why. The outlet reported that it's unclear if the Dream contracted for those dates at State Farm Arena, which is a more appropriate venue for a Finals game.

"Perhaps it was assumed that the Dream would not make it this far. Perhaps, our place in the Finals was not accounted for. Whatever the reason, the reality is that we are here. We earned our place in the Finals, and our city deserves the opportunity to show up for its team," the letter continued.

"Playing a midday game on a Thursday is not what we would have chosen and not what we fought for," the owners wrote. "And as much as we have great affection and nostalgia for Gateway Center Arena, we believed that our fans and the city wanted the opportunity to be a part of this historic series, and to see it played on a world-class stage. That meant State Farm Arena."

"We are grateful to everyone who helped make that possible, especially our partners — the Atlanta Hawks and State Farm Arena — who stepped up by adjusting their schedule on the fly, not once, but three times," the owners continued. "And what a celebration it has been: a party, a concert and incredible Dream basketball all rolled into one. That is what Atlanta supporting Atlanta looks like."

"The Hawks and the Dream are different teams with different histories, but we share a city, a community, and a responsibility to help Atlanta shine on the biggest stages. When one of us has an opportunity to make history, we all want to see it happen," the letter added.

"We have built something special here, powered by our players, our fans, our partners, and a city that believes in what we are doing. We intend to keep building. We intend to keep winning. And we expect the opportunities, planning, and consideration afforded to us to reflect the level at which we compete," the owners concluded. "We are proud to represent Atlanta. We are proud to be in the Finals. And we are grateful for the way this city has rallied around us."

The Atlanta Dream have one famous supporter: Flava Flav , who posted a letter on X on Tuesday, October 27, for those who want to be excused from work or school to attend. "Thursday is a paid holiday. Because Flavor Flav said so," he captioned the image.

The Golden State Valkyries lead the Finals 3-2. The teams will face off at 12:30 p.m. on October 29 for Game 6, which is sold out, according to an October 28 Instagram post from the State Farm Arena. If necessary, Game 7 will take place at 8 p.m. at the Valkyries' home court, Chase Center in San Francisco.

articles.title: UConn women's basketball alum Barbara Turner to make head coaching debut with Unrivaled
articles.summary: Joining Turner on Unrivaled's 2027 coaching staff is former CT Sun associate head coach Roneeka Hodges.
articles.body:
While the Connecticut Sun franchise has departed the state and found its spot in the WNBA team graveyard, its presence still lives on.

Not only in Houston, where the team has been rebranded as the Houston Comets, but also in Miami with Unrivaled.

Unrivaled, the 3x3 league co-founded by UConn women's basketball greats Breanna Stewart and Napheesa Collier, announced its list of 2027 head coaches Wednesday morning, and two have ties to the Sun. Former Sun associate head coach Roneeka Hodges will resume her role as Phantom BC's coach, while former Husky and Sun player Barbara Turner will make her head coaching debut, leading Hive BC.

The league, which begins season three this January, also welcomes back coaches Nola Henry (Rose BC), Andrew Wade (Laces BC), Zach O'Brien (Mist BC), Teresa Weatherspoon (Vinyl BC), and Sed Everett (Player Pool) while introducing new head coaches Pokey Chatman (Lunar Owls BC) and Jarell Christian (Breeze BC).

"We're proud to welcome back so many talented coaches who have been with Unrivaled since our inaugural season and for the foundation they continue to help build," said Unrivaled President of Basketball Clare Duwelius in a release. "Adding new coaches with fresh perspectives further strengthens this group, whose breadth of experience will continue to elevate the best players in the world. ... We're excited for what's ahead in season three."

Hodges was named the 2026 Unrivaled Coach of the Year after leading Phantom to a league-best 11-3 record and championship appearance. Despite losing the championship to Mist, Hodges helped Phantom lead the league in assists (14.6 per game) and average the fewest amount of turnovers per game (7.1). The 2027 season is her second with Unrivaled.

Hodges has ties not only to the Sun but also to the Comets. The former Florida State star was drafted No. 15 overall in 2005 by Houston (before the franchise's fold in 2008) and played three seasons for the Comets. In 2024, she helped lead the New York Liberty to its first WNBA Championship before joining the Sun staff ahead of the 2025 season. Hodges spent two years as an associate head coach for Connecticut. The new Houston team has yet to announce its coaching staff for the 2027 WNBA season.

This is Turner's first-ever head coaching gig after being an assistant coach in the NBA, NBA G League, and WNBA. She just finished her second season as an assistant coach with the Washington Mystics. Turner led UConn to back-to-back national championships in 2003 and 2004. She was named the 2005 Big East Tournament Most Outstanding Player and is No. 24 on UConn's all-time career scoring list with 1,629 points.

Hodges and Turner teamed up on the Comets for the 2007 season. Turner played her final WNBA season with the Sun in 2008 before finishing her playing career overseas.

Unrivaled's 2027 season starts on Jan. 8 with a doubleheader in Boston at TD Garden. The league has yet to announce its full schedule (including which teams will be playing in Boston) or its rosters for the upcoming season. Former UConn stars Stewart, Collier, Paige Bueckers, Aaliyah Edwards, Tiffany Hayes and Gabby Williams are signed to play in the league's upcoming season.

articles.title: Anthony Edwards' Knee Injury, Recovery Timeline Detailed by Wolves' Connelly in New Video
articles.summary: Minnesota Timberwolves president of basketball operations Tim Connelly provided an update on star Anthony Edwards but refrained from putting a possible timeline on his return.
articles.body:
Minnesota Timberwolves president of basketball operations Tim Connelly provided an update on star Anthony Edwards but refrained from putting a possible timeline on his return.

Connelly said Edwards' knee injury is "not something we are concerned with long term."

ESPN's Shams Charania reported Tuesday that Edwards would be sidelined for up to two months after undergoing an arthroscopic procedure on his right knee.

The Timberwolves have been hopeful that the four-time All-Star can return "sometime in December or so" following the surgery, per Jon Krawczynski of The Athletic.

Edwards initially dealt with patellofemoral pain syndrome , also known as runner's knee, during his 2025-26 campaign. He was limited to a career-low 61 regular-season games due to the right knee issue before a hyperextended left knee caused him to miss two playoff contests.

Still, the 25-year-old opened the 2026-27 season on a high note before his knee surgery.

In Edwards' first four games of the year, he averaged 33.3 points, 4.8 rebounds, 3.5 assists and 2.0 steals per game while shooting 48.1 percent from the field and 40.0 percent from three-point territory.

Until he's able to return, LaMelo Ball and Ayo Dosunmu should continue to operate in larger roles leading Minnesota's offense.

The Timberwolves are off to a 3-1 start on the season.
